::: {.callout-important title="Core finding"}
On the IFLA Library Map of the World metric frame, Ahmedabad's M.J. Library
network is weak on service-point density and extremely weak on registered users
and loans. The cleanest headline is **one registered M.J. Library network member
per roughly 264 Ahmedabad residents**.
:::

## What This Report Measures

This report uses IFLA's Library Map of the World framing as the primary comparator
standard. IFLA's Data Lab is built around core statistics such as service points,
registered users, physical visits, physical loans, eBook loans, audio book loans,
downloads, staff, volunteers, and internet access. IFLA also supports per-1-million
population views, which is the right denominator for city comparison.

Finance is still included, but only as a secondary context. PPP dollars do not
measure library performance; they help interpret the scale of public commitment
behind the service.

## Executive Findings

Ahmedabad's M.J. Library network looks less like a citywide public reading system
and more like a flagship collection and institutional archive with weak active-use
conversion.

Latest M.J. Library disclosure data for 2025-26 reports:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---:|
| Collection items | 811,093 |
| New additions | 4,859 |
| Registered network members | 26,834 |
| Annual members | 505 |
| Lifetime members | 25,574 |
| Gyanvihar members | 755 |
| Annual circulation | 96,491 |
| Collection refresh | 0.60% |

Against the SevenT4 Ahmedabad ward-population denominator of 7,078,533 residents,
that is only 0.379 percent registered membership penetration.

The financing is overwhelmingly municipal. In 2025-26, M.J. Library reports a
budget of Rs 22.7675 crore, of which Rs 21.9255 crore is AMC grant and Rs 0.8420
crore is library income. AMC therefore funds 96.30 percent of the reported budget.

### Metric status summary

| Metric category | Value | Confidence | Status |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Registered membership penetration | 0.379% | High | Low reach |
| Residents per registered member | 263.8 | High | Access gap |
| Annual circulation | 96,491 | High | Critical decline |
| Collection refresh | 0.60% | High | Slow renewal |

Data confidence is high where values are directly reported or arithmetically
derived from reported values. Missing IFLA fields are not inferred; they are
reported as explicit data gaps.

## IFLA-Aligned Comparator

\small

| IFLA metric | Ahmedabad / M.J. Library | Toronto Public Library | Reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Service points per 1M residents | 8.8 using 62 AMC library points | 34.0-36.5 using 100 branches + 2 bookmobiles | Toronto has about 4x the service-point density. |
| Registered users per 1M residents | 3,790.9 | Not published on current TPL page | Ahmedabad's registered-user base is extremely low. |
| New registrations per 1M residents | 71.3 annual M.J. members | 78,423-84,195 card registrations | TPL's annual registration flow is over 1,000x larger per resident. |
| Physical visits per 1M residents | No disclosed visit count | 4.47m-4.80m branch visits | Ahmedabad cannot yet be compared on this IFLA metric. |
| Loans per 1M residents | 13,631.5 circulation | 9.33m-10.02m borrowings | TPL records roughly 685x more borrowing per resident. |
| eBook/audio/download metrics | Not captured | Not separated on current TPL page | Add to next extraction schema. |
| Staff, volunteers, internet access | Not captured | Not counted on current TPL page | Add to next extraction schema. |

\normalsize

The strongest standard metric is loans per population. Ahmedabad reports 13,631.5
circulations per million residents. Toronto reports 9.33-10.02 million borrowings
per million residents. The Toronto figure is all material borrowing rather than a
physical-only IFLA line, but the gap is too large to be explained by classification
alone.

The second strongest standard metric is service points per population. Ahmedabad
has 8.8 service points per million residents using the authoritative AMC library
layer. Toronto has 34.0-36.5 per million when branches and bookmobiles are counted
as service points. Ahmedabad's physical access footprint is about one quarter of
Toronto's on this denominator.

## Ahmedabad Trend

Membership growth needs a careful reading. The headline network member count rose
from 20,764 in 2015-16 to 26,834 in 2025-26, a 29.2 percent increase. But annual
members peaked at 3,194 in 2018-19 and fell to 505 by 2025-26. The 2025-26
membership base is therefore lifetime-heavy: lifetime members account for about
95 percent of the network roll.

Circulation is the clearest demand-capture warning. The network reported 193,138
circulations in 2015-16, 207,360 in 2016-17, and 212,397 in 2017-18. By 2025-26,
it reported 96,491. Reported circulation has roughly halved from the pre-2020
level.

## Finance and User Fees

M.J. Library's 2025-26 budget table reports:

| Finance line | Rs crore | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| Total budget | 22.7675 | 100.00% |
| AMC grant | 21.9255 | 96.30% |
| Library income | 0.8420 | 3.70% |
| Books | 0.2500 | 1.10% of total budget |
| All reading material | 0.3275 | 1.44% of total budget |
| Establishment/payroll | 14.0415 | 61.67% of total budget |
| Maintenance | 1.5550 | 6.83% of total budget |
| IT automation | 0.7600 | 3.34% of total budget |
| Capital | 1.5800 | 6.94% of total budget |
| New plans | 2.7100 | 11.90% of total budget |

The "library income" line should not be treated as pure user-fee revenue. It is
an upper bound for self-income and may include membership fees, reading-room
charges, auditorium rent, deposits, fines, interest, and miscellaneous receipts.

Even a generous 2025-26 membership-fee estimate comes to about Rs 17.335 lakh,
or 0.761 percent of total budget and 20.6 percent of disclosed library income.
Fees therefore do not fund the library. Their practical role is closer to access
rationing and administrative filtering inside a system already paid for by AMC.

## PPP Finance Context

PPP conversion uses the World Bank `PA.NUS.PPP` indicator:

| Country | Conversion factor used | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| India | Rs 20.4219876 per international dollar | Latest checked value available for India was 2024; used for M.J. Library 2025-26. |
| Canada | CAD 1.150472 per international dollar | 2024 value; matched to TPL's 2024 finance and usage data. |

Supplemental finance comparison:

| Metric | Ahmedabad / M.J. Library | Toronto Public Library |
|---|---:|---:|
| Public budget, PPP | $11.15m intl. | $254.7m intl. |
| Budget per resident, PPP | $1.57 | $85-$91 |
| Budget per borrow, PPP | $115.5 | $9.1 |

Toronto spends roughly 54x more per resident in PPP terms. But it also records
roughly 685x more borrowing per resident. That means Ahmedabad's problem is not
only underfunding; it is also weak conversion of public subsidy and collection
stock into visible public use.

## Data Gaps

The M.J. Library disclosures do not yet expose several IFLA metrics in a clean
standard format:

- physical visits;
- eBook loans;
- audio book loans;
- downloads;
- libraries with internet access;
- full-time staff;
- volunteers.

The next extraction schema should add these fields explicitly:
`ifla_metric_name`, `ifla_metric_scope`, `metric_value`,
`population_denominator`, `per_1m_population`, `source_page`, and `confidence`.

## Ward-Level Gap Queue

The dashboard draft identified the next spatial-analysis queue rather than a
completed catchment result. The priority is to join library locations to bus,
BRTS, metro, schools and colleges, population density, and ward deprivation, then
classify high-population wards with weak library catchment access.

Initial priority candidates to test:

| Ward candidate | Priority | Why it is queued |
|---|---|---|
| Lambha | High | Very high population and previous service-gap signals. |
| Ramol Hathijan | High | Very high population and previous service-gap signals. |
| Vastral | High | High population with weak public-library access signals. |

These are queued candidates, not final catchment findings. The final ward-gap
table should only be published after the spatial join is run and source
confidence is attached to each ward row.

## Working Conclusions

1. M.J. Library is important, but the data makes it look like a flagship-plus-archive
   institution more than a citywide public reading network.
2. The membership number is not an active-user number. It is lifetime-heavy and
   should be reported alongside annual members, new members, renewals, and active
   borrowers.
3. AMC grant dependence is not a weakness by itself. Public libraries are public
   goods. The weakness is that a 96 percent public-funded network has such low
   public reach.
4. User fees are fiscally marginal and socially material. They do not fund the
   library, but they can still deter use.
5. Ward/catchment analysis should be the next step, beginning with Lambha, Ramol
   Hathijan, and Vastral as high-priority candidates for verification.
